More frequent heatwaves are changing how winegrowers work. In Alentejo, one of Portugal's hottest regions, an estate now harvests at night to improve working conditions.
In the pitch-dark night, the grapes are lit up by the beams from helmets and tractors moving across the fields. At Herdade das Servas, an estate in Portugal’s Alentejo region, the grape harvest now takes place at night. And those who work here do not seem to mind.

Maria Jerónima Mendes is one of dozens of people involved in picking the grapes. She told AFP that the change has not disrupted the work and that, thanks to the light she carries with her, she even "sees the grapes better than in daylight".
"It sounds like a lie, but it isn’t. The body gets used to turning day into night and night into day," she explained.
On this estate, picking grapes at night began in 2024 as a test and has been adopted as standard practice since last year. It is a response to intense heat and increasingly frequent extreme weather events.
"This night-time harvest came from the need to provide better working conditions for the teams, because Alentejo has a very harsh climate in summer," Renato Neves told AFP. For this winegrower and oenologist, harvesting at night is no longer just an option: it is becoming an unavoidable reality for producers in the region.
"In future, it will be inevitable. In my view, more and more companies will start picking at night, because it is going to become very hard for people to carry on harvesting from 11 am or midday, in temperatures of 40, 41 or 42 degrees," he said.
Alentejo is one of the hottest and driest regions in mainland Portugal, where summer highs of between 35 and 38 degrees are common and peaks are even higher during heatwaves, episodes that specialists increasingly link to climate change.

South Korea's aquaculture sector is facing mounting losses as a prolonged marine heatwave pushes sea temperatures to record levels, killing millions of farmed fish, reports The Korea Times.
At Dara Port in Tongyeong, vessels have been arriving loaded with dead fish and crews have been taking more than 30 minutes to clear each vessel.
"This is the sixth boatload of dead fish from our farm alone today," one farmer said. "More than 30% of the fish at our one-hectare cage farm have died, and we've already lost more than KRW 500 million ($371,500)."
Preliminary data from the country's ministry of oceans and fisheries show 13.53m farmed fish across 455 farms had died as of Sept. 4. In South Gyeongsang province alone, losses have reached 7.69m fish and abalone.
But the trend is worsening.
Over the past five years, high water temperatures have killed more than 125m farmed fish, causing losses of KRW 205.56 billion. Sea temperatures hit 28.56 degrees Celsius in early August, the highest on record for that period.
"This year's alerts escalated faster than last year," said Kim Hyung-chul, senior researcher and scientist at the National Institute of Fisheries Science. "Seawater temperatures are rising more rapidly."
Industry sources said support remains focused on limited compensation, while experts are calling for changes such as heat-tolerant breeds, deeper-water farming and a shift to more resilient species.

The Court of Appeal has ordered Maltapost to pay a €10,000 fine imposed by the Malta Communications Authority (MCA) after the postal operator failed to meet its next-day delivery targets, rejecting the company’s defence that summer heatwaves constituted a “force majeure”.
In a judgment handed down by Mr Justice Lawrence Mintoff, the court confirmed an earlier decision by the Administrative Review Tribunal.
The dispute centred on the financial year 2018-2019, during which Maltapost achieved a 93.21% success rate for delivering local single-piece mail by the next working day. This fell short of the strict 95% target established by the MCA.
Maltapost appealed the MCA’s compensation demand, arguing that the regulator failed to grant a temporary concession for 65 working days during July and August 2019 when the “feels like” temperatures exceeded 32°C. The postal operator claimed these extreme temperatures amounted to a force majeure event that severely impacted its delivery performance and forced the implementation of alternative working hours to protect staff.
However, the court dismissed this argument, noting that high summer temperatures in Malta are the norm and do not make the delivery of mail absolutely impossible, which is the strict legal threshold required to declare a force majeure. Meteorological data presented during the proceedings proved there were only two official heatwaves during that summer, lasting just three days each in June and July.
The court ruled that these isolated heatwaves did not justify Maltapost’s request for a blanket 65-day concession. The 95% delivery target already includes a 5% leeway specifically designed to accommodate exceptional factors, unexpected delays, and unforeseeable circumstances.
Maltapost also attempted to invalidate the penalty by arguing that its shortfall fell within the performance study’s statistical margin of error. But judge Mintoff rejected this mathematical defence, ruling that applying the margin of error to excuse missed targets would lower the expected standards, render the quality of service reports useless, and defeat the purpose of the regulatory framework.
The court also threw out a late claim by Maltapost that the delivery data was skewed because two of the anonymous panellists used to test the mail service had duplicate door numbers in their respective streets, leading to misdeliveries.
The judge noted this alleged discrepancy was only discovered by Maltapost’s contractors in 2022, years after the 2019 financial period in question, and lacked sufficient corroborating evidence to overturn the study’s findings.
Finally, the court dismissed Maltapost’s complaint that the €10,159 sum was disproportionate and unfairly close to the maximum legal administrative fine of €11,645.
The judgment clarified that the amount is not a punitive fine, but rather a civil compensation payment calculated through a strict mathematical formula set out in the MCA’s 2005 collective compensation scheme. The Court of Appeal rejected all seven of Maltapost’s grievances, confirming the Tribunal’s decision in its entirety, and ordered the company to bear all legal costs for the appeal.

As per the India Meteorological Department placing parts of central and southern India under its highest rainfall warning, a wider belt spanning eastern and northeastern states remains under a heavy-rain fall, keeping weather preparedness firmly in focus.
Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued red alert for extremely heavy rainfall over isolated places of Chhattisgarh, Coastal Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Telangana for the next two days beginning September 23,2026. The Met Department has predicted heavy rainfall over Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Meghalaya, Bihar, Jharkhand, Kerala, Maharashtra, West Bengal and Sikkim today ( September 24,2026). The weather department also forecast thunderstorms accompanied with highly gusty winds over Madhya Pradesh and Parts of North-East today.
Four States Under Red Alert
The IMD has issued a red alert for extremely heavy rainfall at isolated places in Chhattisgarh, Coastal Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Telangana over the following two days. The warning indicates the possibility of intense rainfall concentrated over specific locations rather than uniformly across the states.
Heavy Rain Extends Across a Wider Belt
The weather system is expected to affect a much broader region. Heavy rainfall has been forecast across Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Meghalaya, Bihar, Jharkhand, Kerala, Maharashtra, West Bengal and Sikkim during the next phase of the forecast period.
The spread of the warning across eastern, northeastern, central and southern parts of the country points to a continuing period of unsettled weather, requiring local conditions and updated forecasts to be monitored closely.
Thunderstorms Add Another Risk
Alongside rainfall, the IMD has forecast thunderstorms accompanied by highly gusty winds over Madhya Pradesh and parts of the Northeast. The combination makes weather conditions potentially disruptive beyond areas under the rainfall alerts themselves.
Delhi Expected to Remain Largely Clear
The national capital is forecast to see mostly clear skies with no rain. Delhi’s maximum temperature is expected to remain around 34–35°C, while the minimum is likely to range between 23–25°C.
Preparedness Must Follow the Forecast
The significance of the warning lies not only in where rain is expected, but in how quickly local conditions can change. With extremely heavy rainfall forecast in four states and heavy rain across several others, continued monitoring of official advisories remains essential as the weather system evolves.

Maharashtra Ganesh Visarjan Weather: Mumbai, Pune, Satara, Sangli, Nagpur, Nashik, Ratnagiri to witness rain in next 24 hours, IMD says…
Parts of Maharashtra have received moderate rainfall over the past 24 hours. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued a yellow alert for some districts and an orange alert for others. Meanwhile, dry weather is likely to prevail in a few parts of the state.
New Delhi: Lord Ganesha is worshipped with special rituals from the Chaturthi Tithi of the Shukla Paksha in the month of Bhadrapada until Anant Chaturdashi. This period marks the celebration of Ganesh Chaturthi, also known as the Ganesh Mahotsav. On Chaturthi, idols of Lord Ganesha are installed in homes and pandals, and on Anant Chaturdashi, the idols are immersed in water following traditional rituals.
According to Drik Panchang, the Chaturdashi Tithi for Ganesh Visarjan will begin at 11:18 PM on September 24 and end at 11:06 PM on September 25. Therefore, Ganesh Visarjan will be performed on Friday, September 25.
Parts of Maharashtra have witnessed moderate rains in last 24 hours. While yellow rain alert has been forecast for some districts and an orange alert has been forecast for others. In some places, the weather is more likely to remain dry. Know the overall weather forecast of the state on September 24, 2026 as follows.
Here are some of the key details:
Light rain is expected in Palghar, Thane, Mumbai, Raigad in Konkan.
A yellow alert for rain is expected in Sindhudurg district.
Dry weather is expected in Dhule and Nandurbar in North Maharashtra.
Light rain with lightning is likely in Nashik.
Light to moderate rain with lightning is expected in Ghatmatha area of Nashik.
Light rain with lightning is likely in Ahilyanagar.
In western Maharashtra, light to moderate rainfall with lightning is expected in Pune, Pune Ghatmatha, Satara Ghatmatha.
A yellow alert is being forecast for these districts. There is a possibility of light rainfall with lightning in Sangli and Solapur.
In the Marathwada division, a yellow alert for rain is forecast for the districts of Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, Jalna, Parbhani, Beed, Hingoli, Latur, and Dharashiv.
In Vidarbha, a yellow alert for rain is expected in Akola, Amravati, Bhandara, Buldhana, Gondia and Wardha districts.
An orange alert for rain is expected in Nagpur, Gadchiroli, Yavatmal and Chandrapur districts.
Delhi records maximum temperature of 34.4 degrees Celsius
Delhi recorded a maximum temperature of 34.4 degrees Celsius on Wednesday, 2.1 notches above seasonal average, as the Southwest Monsoon withdrew from the capital, two days ahead of its normal withdrawal date of September 25, according to the Indian Meteorological Department (IMD).
The minimum settled at 24.8 degrees Celsius, 0.9 degree above normal. The IMD has forecast mainly clear skies throughout Thursday, with maximum and minimum temperatures expected to settle around 34 and 24 degrees Celsius, respectively.
The relative humidity stood at 58 per cent at 5:30 pm. The weather office said the Southwest Monsoon withdrew from the entire national capital region, besides most parts of Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, and some parts of Uttar Pradesh and Gujarat, on Wednesday.
